sections.title: Christians and spices
sections.intro_md:
On 20 May 1498 three Portuguese ships anchored off the Malabar coast, near Calicut. They had sailed for ten months, around the bottom of Africa, to reach this beach. According to the anonymous journal of the voyage, the first man sent ashore met two merchants from Tunis who spoke Castilian. Their first question was, roughly, what the devil had brought them. The answer has become famous: **"We come in search of Christians and spices."**

The spices were mostly black pepper, a dried berry from a vine that grew in the hills behind the coast. Within a decade Portugal had forts on that coast. Within a century the Dutch and the English had joined the race, and companies built to buy pepper and nutmeg had become the first great multinational corporations, with private armies.

That is the argument of today. Food is not the background to history. It is often the cause. The search for flavour drew the map of the world. The need for calories built cities, empires and slave plantations. The lack of it toppled kings. By tonight you should be able to look at a plate of rajma chawal or a cup of chai and name the empires, ships, famines and scientists hiding inside it.

spotlights.name: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded Portuguese commander in a dark cap; a plain stone pillar on Kappad beach, north of Kozhikode, marks the landing.
spotlights.story_md: Da Gama left Lisbon in July 1497 with four ships and about 170 men. Arab and Gujarati traders had used the monsoon winds of the Indian Ocean for centuries; a local pilot helped guide him across from East Africa in about 23 days. At Calicut the Zamorin, the Hindu ruler, was unimpressed by his gifts of cloth, hats and washbasins. Da Gama still went home with pepper and cinnamon. Fewer than half his men survived. Yet the cargo is often said to have paid for the voyage many times over, and the sea route he opened let Europe bypass the Venetian and Arab middlemen who had controlled the spice trade.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It opened the direct sea route that pulled India into four centuries of European trade and conquest.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten months at sea, half the crew dead, for a hold full of peppercorns.

spotlights.name: Black pepper
spotlights.spot_it: Green berries hanging in long strings from a climbing vine, dried in the sun until they turn black and wrinkled.
spotlights.story_md: Black pepper is the unripe fruit of *Piper nigrum*, a vine native to the Western Ghats. Peppercorns were found stuffed into the nostrils of the mummy of Ramesses II, who died in 1213 BCE, which means pepper had already crossed from India to Egypt. Rome imported so much that it had a special warehouse district for spices, the horrea piperataria. In 408 CE, when the Visigoth king Alaric besieged Rome, his ransom included 3,000 pounds of pepper beside the gold and silver. In medieval Europe it was sometimes accepted in place of rent, and the English phrase 'peppercorn rent' survives today for a token payment.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The world's most traded spice set the routes, wars and companies of the early modern world.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Pharaoh took Indian pepper to the afterlife, up his nose.

sections.title: The numbers that matter
sections.intro_md:
Food history is world history for a simple reason: for almost all of human time, getting enough to eat was the main thing most people did. Until the 19th century, in most societies, well over half of all workers were farmers. Food decided where people lived, how many could live there, who ruled them, and what they fought over.

A few numbers set the scale. Humans have eaten thousands of plants, and the FAO counts more than **50,000 edible species**, yet just **three grasses**, rice, maize and wheat, provide about **60 percent** of the world's food energy. Farming began about **12,000 years ago**, independently in at least seven or eight places. After 1492 the crops of two hemispheres swapped in about a century. About **12.5 million** Africans were shipped across the Atlantic as slaves, most of them to grow sugar. Synthetic fertiliser made by the Haber-Bosch process now supports roughly **half** of humanity. And in 2025, by the UN's latest count, **645 million** people still went hungry.

Hold those numbers. Every section today explains one of them.

spotlights.name: Rice, wheat and maize
spotlights.spot_it: Three grasses: rice in flooded paddies, wheat in golden dry fields, maize on tall stalks with cobs wrapped in husks.
spotlights.story_md: Rice was tamed in the Yangtze valley of China, wheat in the hills of south-east Turkey and the Fertile Crescent, maize in the Balsas valley of south-west Mexico. Each became the base of a civilisation: rice of China, Japan and the Bengal delta; wheat of Mesopotamia, Rome and the Punjab; maize of the Maya and Aztecs. Each also shaped society in a different way. Rice paddies need water shared by a whole village. Wheat stores well and can be taxed. Today the three supply about 60 percent of the calories humans eat, which means a single bad harvest in a few countries can move prices across the planet.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Three plants now carry most of humanity, which makes the world both well fed and fragile.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three grasses, sixty percent of every calorie.

sections.title: The first farmers
sections.intro_md:
For about 95 percent of human history, everyone was a forager. Then, from about 12,000 years ago, people in a handful of regions began to plant seeds and keep animals. It happened independently in the Fertile Crescent (wheat, barley, lentils, sheep, goats), China (rice and millet), Mesoamerica (maize, beans, squash), the Andes (potato, quinoa, llama), New Guinea (taro, banana), the African Sahel (sorghum) and parts of South Asia.

Farming was not an obvious improvement. Skeletons of early farmers are often shorter and show more tooth decay and disease than those of foragers. But farming produced more food per acre, so it supported more people, and more people could outnumber their neighbours. Stored grain could be counted, taxed and stolen. Out of that came writing, cities, armies and kings.

The surprises in this section: a temple that may be older than farming, a wheat that can be traced to one mountain, a grass that became corn, and the world's oldest dentistry, in Balochistan.

spotlights.name: Gobekli Tepe
spotlights.spot_it: Rings of giant T-shaped limestone pillars on a hilltop, carved with foxes, boars, snakes and vultures.
spotlights.story_md: When the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt began digging this hill near Sanliurfa in south-east Turkey in 1995, he found monumental pillars up to about 5.5 metres tall, raised around 11,500 years ago, about 6,000 years before Stonehenge. There were no signs of farmed crops at the start. Schmidt's line, 'first came the temple, then the city', suggested that gathering people for feasts or rituals might have pushed them to settle and farm. Later work has found houses and water cisterns, so the site was not only a temple. But the question it raised remains: did people farm to feed gatherings, rather than gather because they farmed?
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned the story of civilisation upside down: monuments may have come before agriculture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six thousand years before Stonehenge, hunters were raising pillars and possibly brewing for a party.

spotlights.name: Einkorn wheat
spotlights.spot_it: A slim, flat wheat ear with a single grain per spikelet and long whiskers, smaller than modern bread wheat.
spotlights.story_md: In 1997 a team led by Manfred Heun compared the DNA of hundreds of wild and farmed einkorn lines and traced the domesticated form to the **Karacadag mountains** of south-east Turkey, only about 30 kilometres from Gobekli Tepe. The key change was tiny: wild wheat shatters, dropping its seeds when ripe, which is good for the plant and bad for the harvester. A mutant whose ears stayed intact could only spread if people sowed it. Every time farmers harvested and replanted, they selected for that mutant. Domestication was not a plan. It was a feedback loop between a grass and a sickle.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how domestication worked: humans and plants changed each other.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first wheat was a mutant that forgot how to scatter its own seeds.

spotlights.name: Teosinte, the wild ancestor of maize
spotlights.spot_it: A wild Mexican grass with a tiny ear of 5 to 12 rock-hard kernels, next to a maize cob of hundreds.
spotlights.story_md: For decades botanists could not believe that maize came from teosinte; the two look like different plants. Genetic studies in the early 2000s settled it: maize descends from a teosinte of the Balsas river valley in south-west Mexico, domesticated about 9,000 years ago. A few genes made a huge difference. One, called *tb1*, turned a bushy plant into a single stalk; another freed the kernels from their stony cases. Over thousands of years Mesoamerican farmers built a cob that cannot reproduce without people pulling it apart and planting the seeds. Maize is now the world's largest crop by tonnage.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most produced grain on Earth is an artificial plant that cannot survive without us.
spotlights.memory_hook: A grass with a dozen stony seeds became the cob on your plate.

spotlights.name: Mehrgarh
spotlights.spot_it: Mud-brick ruins on the Kachi plain at the foot of the Bolan Pass, Balochistan, with painted pottery from later levels.
spotlights.story_md: Mehrgarh, excavated by a French team led by Jean-Francois Jarrige from 1974, is the oldest known farming village in South Asia. Its people grew barley and wheat and kept goats, sheep and humped zebu cattle by about 7000 BCE. In 2006 the journal Nature reported something extraordinary: eleven molars from nine adults, between about 9,000 and 7,500 years old, had neat holes drilled into them while the people were alive. It is the earliest known dentistry. The likely tool was a flint bow drill, the same one used to make beads. Mehrgarh is a direct ancestor of the farming culture that later built the Indus cities.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It roots the Indian subcontinent's food story in its own Neolithic, not a borrowed one.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first farmers in South Asia also had the first dentists.

spotlights.name: The Andean potato

where.label: Lake Titicaca region, Peru and Bolivia

spotlights.spot_it: Knobbly tubers in purple, red, yellow and speckled skins, piled in a market in Peru or Bolivia.
spotlights.story_md: The potato was domesticated near Lake Titicaca, between modern Peru and Bolivia. Andean farmers grew it at heights where little else survives, and bred thousands of varieties, each fitted to a slope, a frost pattern or a soil. They also invented one of the first freeze-dried foods, **chuno**: potatoes left out on frosty nights, trampled to squeeze out water and dried in the sun, which could keep for years. That storage fed the armies and road crews of the Inca empire. Peru's International Potato Center in Lima keeps a gene bank of more than 4,000 Andean varieties today.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without the Andean potato, the population of Europe after 1700 would look very different.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Inca empire marched on freeze-dried potatoes.

sections.title: Bread, beer and the first states
sections.intro_md:
Once grain could be stored, someone had to count it. Some of the oldest writing on Earth, from Uruk in Mesopotamia around 3300 to 3000 BCE, is not poetry or law. It is accounting: tallies of barley, sheep and beer. Workers in early states were often paid in food. Builders, soldiers and scribes received rations of bread and beer, and the ration lists are some of our best records of ordinary life.

Grain also explains the shape of Rome. By the time of Augustus the city held perhaps a million people, far more than the land around it could feed. Grain came by sea from Sicily, North Africa and above all Egypt, and from 58 BCE about 200,000 citizens received free grain each month. An emperor who let the bread run out risked a riot. The Roman poet Juvenal sneered that the people wanted only two things: **bread and circuses**.

This section is about the objects that survive from that world: a beer tablet, a loaf from Pompeii, and an entire hill made of broken oil jars.

spotlights.name: The beer ration tablet
spotlights.spot_it: A small clay tablet from southern Iraq with pictographs: a human head eating from a bowl, and a pointed jar, the sign for beer.
spotlights.story_md: This proto-cuneiform tablet in the British Museum records an allocation of beer. The sign for a ration was a head beside a bowl; the sign for beer was a tall jar with a pointed base. Mesopotamians drank beer through long straws to avoid the husks floating on top, and seals show people sharing a jar. Beer was food: thick, nutritious and safer than some water. Around 1800 BCE the Hymn to Ninkasi, the goddess of brewing, praised the steps of making it. Some scholars even argue that the desire for beer, not bread, helped push people to grow barley in the first place, though that remains a lively debate.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Writing itself may have been invented to keep track of food and drink.
spotlights.memory_hook: One of the first things humans wrote down was who got how much beer.

spotlights.name: The carbonised loaf of Pompeii
spotlights.when: Baked on or about 24 August 79 CE
spotlights.spot_it: A round, blackened loaf scored into eight wedges, like a pizza, found in an oven at Pompeii.
spotlights.story_md: When Vesuvius erupted, a baker in Herculaneum and several in Pompeii left bread in their ovens. The heat turned it into charcoal and preserved its shape. The loaves are the round Roman *panis quadratus*, cut into segments before baking so they could be torn apart easily, and some carry a stamp. One from Herculaneum is marked as belonging to Celer, slave of Quintus Granius Verus. Pompeii had more than thirty bakeries, many with their own lava-stone mills turned by donkeys. In 2019 the British Museum asked a chef to recreate the loaf; it is chewy, dense and made with emmer-like wheat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a snapshot of how an ordinary Roman city fed itself the day it ended.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two thousand years later, the bread is still portioned for sharing.

spotlights.name: Monte Testaccio
spotlights.spot_it: A grassy hill 35 metres high in southern Rome that, when you look closely, is made entirely of broken pottery.
spotlights.story_md: Monte Testaccio is a rubbish heap of about **53 million** smashed amphorae, the jars that carried olive oil to Rome, mostly from Baetica in southern Spain. Each held about 70 litres; together they represent around 6 billion litres of oil. Oil soaked into the clay and turned rancid, so the jars could not be reused. Workers broke them and stacked the pieces in neat terraces, sprinkling lime to stop the smell. Many shards still carry painted labels with weights, shippers and tax officials, a giant ledger of the Roman food economy. Today restaurants and nightclubs are cut into its base.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest physical proof that Rome lived on food imported from across its empire.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rome threw away so many oil jars that it made a hill.

sections.title: The spice routes
sections.intro_md:
Spices were the luxury goods that made merchants rich and pulled ships across oceans. They were light, did not rot, and could be sold far from home for many times their cost. The routes were old. Monsoon winds, which blow from the south-west in summer and the north-east in winter, let ships cross the Arabian Sea in a matter of weeks. Greek sailors learned the trick around the 1st century BCE, and Roman ships soon sailed from Egypt's Red Sea ports straight to the Malabar coast.

The trade was not all one way. Indian textiles, gems, ivory and pepper went west; Roman gold coins came east, and hoards of them have been found across south India. The Roman writer Pliny complained that India drained the empire of 50 million sesterces a year.

After 1500 the trade turned violent. The Portuguese, then the Dutch, then the English, tried to control the sources rather than just buy from them. The most extreme case was nutmeg, which grew on only a few tiny islands in eastern Indonesia.

spotlights.name: Muziris
spotlights.when: About 1st century BCE to 4th century CE
spotlights.spot_it: A lost Kerala port; today an excavation site at Pattanam near Kodungallur, with brick wharves and Roman amphora shards.
spotlights.story_md: Tamil Sangam poetry describes Yavana (Greek and Roman) ships arriving at Muciri with gold and leaving with pepper. A 2nd-century Greek papyrus, now in Vienna, records a single cargo on the ship *Hermapollon* worth about 9 million sesterces, mostly pepper and spices, enough to buy a large estate in Italy. Pliny wrote that with the south-west monsoon behind them, ships reached Muziris from the Red Sea in about forty days. The port vanished, probably after the Periyar river shifted its course. Excavations at Pattanam since 2007 have found a brick wharf, a canoe and thousands of Mediterranean pottery fragments.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that India was trading pepper for Roman gold 1,500 years before Vasco da Gama.
spotlights.memory_hook: One shipload of Kerala pepper could buy a Roman estate.

spotlights.name: Nutmeg and mace
spotlights.spot_it: A pale fruit that splits to show a dark brown seed wrapped in a lacy scarlet web: the seed is nutmeg, the red web is mace.
spotlights.story_md: Until the 18th century, nutmeg trees grew only on the Banda Islands, a cluster of volcanic specks in eastern Indonesia. In Europe nutmeg was believed to ward off plague and sold for huge mark-ups. The Dutch East India Company wanted all of it. In 1621 its governor-general Jan Pieterszoon Coen invaded the islands. Estimates suggest the native population of about 15,000 fell to around 1,000, through killing, starvation, flight and enslavement. The Dutch replaced them with plantations worked by slaves. Later the company even soaked exported nutmegs in lime so they could not be planted elsewhere. The French smuggled seedlings out anyway in the 1770s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the starkest example of a spice monopoly enforced by mass killing.
spotlights.memory_hook: A seed in a red lace web cost an island its people.

spotlights.name: Run for Manhattan
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny green island, about 3 kilometres long, at the western edge of the Banda group.
spotlights.story_md: Run was England's only foothold in the nutmeg islands, claimed in 1603. The Dutch besieged it for years and finally took it. Meanwhile, in 1664, the English seized the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam on the island of Manhattan and renamed it New York. At the Treaty of Breda in 1667, ending the Second Anglo-Dutch War, each side kept what it held: the Dutch kept Run, the English kept Manhattan. The treaty did not literally swap one for the other, but in effect it did. At the time, many Dutch thought they had the better deal.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how differently the world valued spice and land in the 17th century.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Dutch kept a nutmeg island; the English got stuck with New York.

spotlights.name: The Dutch East India Company (VOC)
spotlights.spot_it: An interlocking V, O and C monogram, painted on cannons, coins and ships' sterns.
spotlights.story_md: The Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie was set up to bring Dutch spice voyages under one company. It sold shares to the public, which made it one of the first companies with tradeable stock, and the Amsterdam exchange grew up around it. The Dutch state gave it the right to wage war, build forts, mint coins and sign treaties in Asia. Over two centuries it sent about a million Europeans to Asia on nearly 5,000 ships. It had trading posts in India too, at Pulicat, Surat, Cochin and Chinsurah. Its business model rested on pepper, nutmeg, cloves and cinnamon, and on violence to keep their prices high.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was a prototype of the multinational company, and it was built on spices.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first great stock-market company traded in nutmeg and had its own army.

sections.title: The great swap after 1492
sections.intro_md:
In 1972 the historian Alfred Crosby gave a name to the biggest ecological event since the Ice Age: the **Columbian Exchange**. Before 1492 the Americas and Afro-Eurasia had been separated for over 10,000 years, and had domesticated almost entirely different plants and animals. Within about a century of Columbus, they were swapped.

From the Americas came maize, potatoes, sweet potatoes, cassava, tomatoes, chillies, cacao, peanuts, vanilla, pineapples, most beans, squash and tobacco. To the Americas went wheat, rice, sugar cane, coffee, bananas, citrus, cattle, pigs, horses, sheep and chickens. So did smallpox, measles and influenza, which killed a large share of the Indigenous population, by many estimates the great majority within a century or so.

The result is that almost no national cuisine today is 'pure'. Italian food without tomatoes, Irish without potatoes, Thai and Indian without chillies, Ghanaian without cassava, and Argentine without beef would all be unrecognisable. The economists Nathan Nunn and Nancy Qian estimate that the potato alone explains about a quarter of the growth in Old World population and urbanisation between 1700 and 1900.

spotlights.name: The chilli comes to India

where.label: Goa, first Indian landfall of the chilli

spotlights.spot_it: Wrinkled red Bhut jolokia pods from Assam and Nagaland, or heaps of dried red Guntur chillies in a market.
spotlights.story_md: Before about 1500 no Indian had ever tasted a chilli. Heat came from black pepper, long pepper and ginger. Chillies were domesticated in Mexico and South America, and the Portuguese brought them to Goa in the 16th century. They spread with astonishing speed because they grow easily and are cheap: a peasant who could not afford pepper could grow chilli in a pot. The Kannada saint-composer Purandara Dasa, who died in 1564, already praised the chilli in a song. Today India is the world's largest producer and exporter of dried chillies, and the Bhut jolokia of the north-east was certified in 2007 as the world's hottest pepper at more than a million Scoville units.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most 'Indian' flavour of all arrived on European ships about 500 years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: No vindaloo before Vasco: the chilli is a Mexican immigrant.

spotlights.name: Frederick the Great and the potato
spotlights.spot_it: A plain stone slab at Sanssouci palace in Potsdam, always scattered with real potatoes left by visitors.
spotlights.story_md: Europeans were suspicious of the potato for two centuries: it was not in the Bible, it grew underground, and its leaves are poisonous. Frederick II of Prussia, who had seen famine, issued a 'potato order' in 1756 telling officials to promote it. A popular legend says he planted a royal potato field and posted guards, so peasants assumed it was valuable and stole the tubers; the story is charming but unproven. In France Antoine-Augustin Parmentier, who had eaten potatoes as a prisoner of war, campaigned for them in the 1770s and 1780s. By the 19th century the potato fed the workers of the industrial revolution. Visitors to Frederick's grave still leave potatoes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a new food spread through politics, propaganda and hunger.
spotlights.memory_hook: A king's grave decorated with potatoes, not flowers.

spotlights.name: The tomato in Italy
spotlights.when: First described in Italy 1548; first sauce recipe 1692
spotlights.spot_it: Long, plum-shaped San Marzano tomatoes, the variety grown on the volcanic soils near Vesuvius and prized for sauce.
spotlights.story_md: The tomato came from western South America and was domesticated in Mexico. It reached Italy by the 1540s, where the botanist Pietro Andrea Mattioli called it *pomi d'oro*, golden apples, which suggests the first ones were yellow. For over a century Italians mostly grew it as a curiosity. Many Europeans distrusted it, partly because it belongs to the nightshade family. The first published Italian recipe for tomato sauce, 'alla spagnuola', in the Spanish style, appeared in Antonio Latini's Naples cookbook in 1692. Pizza with tomato only became common in Naples in the 18th and 19th centuries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The defining ingredient of Italian cooking is younger than the Renaissance.
spotlights.memory_hook: Italy's golden apple was a Mexican import that took 150 years to reach the sauce pan.

spotlights.name: Cacao, money that grew on trees
spotlights.when: Used by Mesoamericans for at least 3,000 years
spotlights.spot_it: Ridged yellow or red pods growing straight from the trunk of a small tree, full of beans wrapped in white pulp.
spotlights.story_md: Mesoamericans drank cacao long before chocolate bars: a bitter, frothy drink, sometimes with chilli and vanilla, poured from a height to raise foam. The Aztecs used cacao beans as small change. A Nahuatl price list from 1545 says a turkey hen cost 100 beans and a tomato cost one. Spaniards added sugar and took it to Europe, where it became a fashionable drink for the rich. The solid chocolate bar only arrived in the 19th century. Today most cacao is grown not in the Americas but in West Africa, with Cote d'Ivoire and Ghana supplying well over half the world's beans.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It moved from Aztec currency to European luxury to a West African cash crop.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Aztec markets, a tomato cost one cacao bean and a turkey a hundred.

sections.title: Coffee: from a Sufi lodge to Chikmagalur
sections.intro_md:
Not every food that changed history crossed the Atlantic. Coffee came out of Ethiopia and was first brewed as a drink by Sufi mystics in Yemen in the 15th century, who used it to stay awake for night prayers. It spread through Mecca, Cairo and Istanbul, where coffee houses became places for news, gossip and politics. Rulers tried to ban them more than once, worried about sedition.

In 17th-century London, coffee houses became the offices of the city: Lloyd's of London, the insurance market, began in Edward Lloyd's coffee house around 1688. Historians have argued that coffee, a stimulant replacing all-day beer, helped make the European Enlightenment sharper and more sober.

Yemen tried to keep a monopoly by exporting only roasted or boiled beans. It failed, and one of the leaks was in India.

spotlights.name: Baba Budan and the seven beans
spotlights.spot_it: A green hill range in Karnataka's Chikmagalur district, covered in coffee bushes under shade trees.
spotlights.story_md: Legend says a Sufi saint named Baba Budan, returning from the Hajj, smuggled seven coffee beans out of Yemen strapped to his chest, and planted them in the hills of Chikmagalur. Seven was a holy number, so the smuggling could be called a religious act. The details are legend, but coffee was certainly growing in these hills by the late 17th century, and the range is now called the Baba Budan Giri. Under the British, plantations spread across Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu. India is now one of the world's top ten coffee producers, and Karnataka grows about 70 percent of India's coffee, much of it exported.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how India entered the world's coffee map, through a saint, not a company.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven beans under a pilgrim's robe started India's coffee.

sections.title: Sugar: the sweetest crime
sections.intro_md:
Sugar cane was domesticated in New Guinea, but it was India that learned to turn its juice into crystals, by about the Gupta period in the 4th to 6th centuries CE. The Sanskrit word **sharkara** (grit, gravel) passed into Persian as shakar, Arabic as sukkar, and English as **sugar**. The Sanskrit **khanda**, a lump, gave English the word **candy**. In 647 the Tang emperor Taizong sent envoys to India specifically to learn how to make sugar.

Sugar became the engine of the most brutal economy in history. Growing and boiling cane is hard, fast work: cut cane spoils within a day or two, so mills ran around the clock. On the Atlantic islands and then in Brazil and the Caribbean, planters solved the labour problem with enslaved Africans. Of the roughly 12.5 million people shipped across the Atlantic between 1501 and 1866, most were destined for sugar colonies. Death rates were so high that many plantations relied on constant new arrivals.

When slavery was abolished in the British Empire in 1834, planters turned to India. Over the next 80 years, about 1.3 million or more Indians signed indentures to work on sugar estates from Mauritius to Fiji to Guyana.

visual.title: Where enslaved Africans were taken (approximate share of arrivals, 1501 to 1866)

spotlights.name: Gur and the Indian invention of sugar

where.label: Uttar Pradesh, India's largest cane state

spotlights.when: Crystal sugar by about 350 to 600 CE
spotlights.spot_it: Cane juice boiling in a wide iron pan over a fire in a field, poured out to set into golden-brown blocks of gur.
spotlights.story_md: Indian texts mention cane sweeteners for over 2,000 years, and soldiers of Alexander's army reported 'reeds that make honey without bees'. Indians learned to boil cane juice down and crystallise it, which made sugar something that could be stored and shipped. That technique travelled with Buddhist monks to China and with Persian and Arab traders to the Mediterranean. In villages across India the old way is still visible every winter: cane is crushed and the juice boiled in open pans to make **gur** (jaggery). India is today the world's largest consumer of sugar and the second-largest producer after Brazil.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India gave the world both the substance and the word.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sugar is a Sanskrit word for gravel; candy is a Sanskrit word for a lump.

spotlights.name: The plantation sugar mill
spotlights.spot_it: A ruined round stone tower on a Caribbean hillside: the base of a windmill that once crushed cane.
spotlights.story_md: Barbados, settled by the English in 1627, was the laboratory of the sugar plantation. By the 1660s it was producing sugar on a vast scale, and the model spread to Jamaica, Saint-Domingue (Haiti) and beyond. The stone windmill towers that dot Barbados and Antigua today housed rollers that crushed cane; the juice ran to a boiling house where enslaved workers ladled it between copper pans in tremendous heat. Saint-Domingue became the richest colony in the world, and the most violent. Its enslaved people rose up in 1791 and founded Haiti in 1804, the only state born from a successful slave revolt.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Caribbean sugar island was a factory before Europe had factories.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tower on a hill crushed cane and lives.

spotlights.name: The Brookes slave ship diagram
spotlights.spot_it: A plan of a ship's hold seen from above, packed with hundreds of tiny drawn figures lying side by side.
spotlights.story_md: Abolitionists in Plymouth and London printed this plan of the Liverpool slave ship Brookes to show what the trade meant. It shows 454 people, the number legally allowed after a 1788 regulation; on one earlier voyage the ship had carried more than 600. Each adult man was allotted a space about 6 feet by 16 inches. Thousands of copies were printed and hung in homes and coffee houses. It is often called one of the most effective political images ever made. Many abolitionists also boycotted slave-grown sugar; around 1791 perhaps 300,000 Britons stopped buying it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed how a single image, and a sugar boycott, could change a nation's mind.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hundreds of people drawn like cargo, so that no one could look away.

spotlights.name: Aapravasi Ghat
spotlights.spot_it: A set of worn basalt steps leading up from the harbour at Port Louis, Mauritius, to the remains of an immigration depot.
spotlights.story_md: After Britain abolished slavery, sugar planters in Mauritius brought indentured workers from India. Between 1849 and 1923 about half a million of them passed through this depot, climbing its 16 steps to be registered and sent to estates. Indentured workers signed contracts, usually for five years, but conditions were often close to slavery, and many never went home. The 'great experiment' started in Mauritius was copied in Trinidad, Guyana, Fiji, Natal and Suriname. That is why Mauritius today has an Indian-origin majority, and why roti and curry are national foods in Trinidad. UNESCO listed the site in 2006.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where the Indian diaspora of the sugar colonies began.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sixteen steps, half a million people, one sugar economy.

sections.title: Tea, opium and empire
sections.intro_md:
In the 18th century Britain fell in love with tea, and almost all of it came from China. China wanted little that Britain made, so Britain paid in silver, and the silver drained away. The East India Company found an answer in Bengal: **opium**. Grown under Company monopoly around Patna and Ghazipur, it was auctioned in Calcutta and smuggled into China by private traders. By the 1820s and 1830s the flow of silver had reversed.

When the Chinese official Lin Zexu destroyed over 1,000 tonnes of seized opium in 1839, Britain went to war. The First Opium War ended in 1842 with the Treaty of Nanking, which opened Chinese ports and handed Hong Kong to Britain. Tea had paid for opium, and opium had paid for tea.

Meanwhile tea also helped start a revolution in America, and a botanist in disguise helped move the whole industry to India. Your cup of chai sits on all of this.

Robert Bruce shown wild tea in Assam by a Singpho chief

Maniram Dewan hanged after the 1857 uprising

spotlights.name: The Boston Tea Party
spotlights.spot_it: A famous 19th-century lithograph of men, some disguised as Mohawk Indians, throwing chests of tea off ships into Boston harbour.
spotlights.story_md: The Tea Act of 1773 was meant to rescue the struggling East India Company by letting it sell tea directly to the American colonies. It actually made tea cheaper, but colonists objected to the principle of a tax set in London and to a monopoly. On the night of 16 December, a group called the Sons of Liberty boarded three ships and dumped **342 chests** of East India Company tea into the harbour. Britain responded with the punishing 'Intolerable Acts', which pushed the colonies toward the War of Independence in 1775. Coffee then gained ground in America as the patriotic drink.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A protest over tea, imported by a company that ruled Bengal, helped trigger American independence.
spotlights.memory_hook: Americans drink coffee partly because of a tax on Indian-company tea.

spotlights.name: The First Opium War
spotlights.spot_it: A painting of an iron steamship, the Nemesis, blasting wooden Chinese war junks in a river battle in 1841.
spotlights.story_md: The war was fought to keep the opium trade open. Britain's new iron steamer **Nemesis**, built for the East India Company, could sail up shallow rivers and outgun Qing junks with ease, a brutal demonstration of industrial power. Troops in the British force included many Indian sepoys. The Treaty of Nanking in 1842 forced China to pay compensation, open five ports and cede Hong Kong island. Chinese historians call the period that followed the 'century of humiliation'. Meanwhile, in British India, opium had become one of the largest sources of government revenue, at times second only to land tax.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Drug money from Indian fields built a colonial economy and humbled the Chinese empire.
spotlights.memory_hook: Britain fought a war so that it could keep selling drugs to buy tea.

spotlights.name: Robert Fortune, tea thief
spotlights.spot_it: A glass-sided wooden Wardian case, the sealed mini-greenhouse that let Fortune ship living tea plants across oceans.
spotlights.story_md: The East India Company wanted to grow tea in its own territory rather than buy from China. In 1848 it hired the Scottish plant hunter Robert Fortune to enter China's closed tea regions, where foreigners were forbidden. Disguised as a Chinese official from a distant province, he collected seeds and plants and learned the secrets of processing, including that green and black tea come from the same plant, processed differently. Using sealed glass Wardian cases as tiny greenhouses, he shipped about 20,000 plants and seedlings to the Himalayas, along with skilled Chinese tea workers. Most of the plants died, but enough survived to help found the Darjeeling tea industry.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was one of the biggest acts of industrial espionage in history, and it moved an industry to India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A botanist in a fake pigtail carried China's tea secrets to Darjeeling.

spotlights.name: The tea gardens of Assam
spotlights.spot_it: Flat-topped waist-high tea bushes in endless rows, shaded by tall trees, with pluckers carrying baskets on their heads.
spotlights.story_md: Tea grew wild in Assam all along. The Singpho people brewed it, and in 1823 the Scottish trader Robert Bruce was shown the plants by a Singpho chief, with the help of the Assamese nobleman Maniram Dewan. British experts were slow to accept that it was real tea. The Assam Company was founded in 1839, and the industry grew on the labour of hundreds of thousands of workers recruited from central and eastern India under harsh contracts. Maniram Dewan, who later started his own gardens, was hanged by the British after the 1857 uprising. India is now the world's second-largest tea producer after China.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made tea an Indian product and created one of India's largest workforces.
spotlights.memory_hook: The British spent decades smuggling tea from China while it grew wild in Assam.

spotlights.name: Masala chai
spotlights.spot_it: Milky brown tea boiled with sugar, ginger and cardamom, poured from a height into small glasses or clay kulhads at a roadside stall.
spotlights.story_md: For most of the colonial period, Indians did not drink much tea. Planters exported it. In the 1900s the Indian Tea Association launched campaigns to build a home market, with promotional tea stalls at railway stations and factories, and demonstrations of how to brew it. Indians made it their own: boiled with milk and sugar, often with spices, which used less leaf and suited local taste. The British-run association reportedly disliked the milky, spiced version because it used less tea. Today India drinks most of the tea it grows, more than a billion kilograms a year, and the chaiwala is a national figure.
spotlights.why_it_matters: An export product built by an empire became a symbol of Indian everyday life.
spotlights.memory_hook: The British sold Indians tea; Indians fixed the recipe.

sections.title: Salt: the tax that lit a fire
sections.intro_md:
Salt is the only rock humans eat, and until refrigeration it was the main way to preserve meat, fish and vegetables. That made it easy to tax: everyone needs it, and it comes from a few places. China had a state salt monopoly from the 2nd century BCE. In France, the hated **gabelle** salt tax forced households to buy a minimum amount at fixed prices; it was one of the grievances of the Revolution and was abolished in 1790.

In India the British ran salt as a monopoly. Making salt from seawater without a licence was a crime. In 1930 that rule gave Gandhi the perfect symbol: a tax that hit the poorest, on something nature gave freely, enforced by a foreign government.

Salt also made fortunes. Under Wieliczka near Krakow, miners worked rock salt from the 13th century until 1996 and carved whole chapels, chandeliers included, out of it; the mine was on UNESCO's first World Heritage list in 1978. And salt gave English the word 'salary', though the story that Roman soldiers were paid in salt is unproven.

visual.title: Salt: the march, the pans, the mine

spotlights.name: The Salt March
spotlights.spot_it: Gandhi, thin, walking stick in hand, leading a line of marchers in white khadi along a dusty road.
spotlights.story_md: Gandhi set out from Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad with 78 chosen followers and walked about 385 kilometres in 24 days to the coastal village of Dandi. On the morning of 6 April he picked up a lump of natural salt from the mud and so broke the Salt Law. Across India people began making and selling salt illegally. Within a year, about 60,000 people had been arrested, including Gandhi himself. The march drew worldwide press coverage; Time magazine named Gandhi its Man of the Year for 1930. The salt tax itself was not abolished until 1946.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned a food tax into the most famous act of civil disobedience of the 20th century.
spotlights.memory_hook: A pinch of mud-salt on a Gujarati beach shook an empire.

spotlights.name: The salt pans of the Little Rann
spotlights.spot_it: A white, cracked, endless flat under a hazy sky, divided into rectangular pans where brine evaporates.
spotlights.story_md: Gujarat produces most of India's salt, roughly three quarters of it. A large share of inland salt comes from the Little Rann of Kutch, a seasonal salt desert where the Agariya community pumps up underground brine and lets the sun evaporate it, from October to April. The work is punishing: years of walking barefoot in brine harden workers' feet so much that it is said they do not burn fully on the funeral pyre. India is the world's third-largest salt producer, after China and the United States, and exports to dozens of countries. Salt from these pans may well be in your kitchen.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's salt still depends on one of its hardest jobs.
spotlights.memory_hook: White desert, barefoot workers, and three quarters of India's salt from one state.

sections.title: When the food ran out
sections.intro_md:
Food shortages have toppled governments for as long as there have been governments. In October 1789 thousands of Paris market women, furious about the price of bread, marched to Versailles and brought the king back to the city. In 2010 and 2011 record world food prices fed the anger behind the Arab Spring; protesters in Egypt chanted for 'bread, freedom, social justice'.

Famine is the extreme case, and its lesson is uncomfortable. The worst famines of the last two centuries were rarely caused by an absolute lack of food. They were caused by who could get it. The economist Amartya Sen, who saw the Bengal famine as a nine-year-old boy, argued that people starve when they lose their **entitlement** to food: when wages collapse, prices soar, or governments stop them buying it. He also noted that no major famine has ever happened in a functioning democracy with a free press.

Ireland in the 1840s and Bengal in 1943 are the two famines the British Empire most needs to answer for.

data.main trigger: Potato blight plus exports and limited relief

spotlights.name: The Great Irish Famine
spotlights.spot_it: Gaunt bronze figures walking along the Liffey quay in Dublin, a sculpture by Rowan Gillespie remembering the emigrants.
spotlights.story_md: By the 1840s about a third of Ireland's population depended almost entirely on one potato variety, the Lumper. In 1845 a mould from the Americas, *Phytophthora infestans*, arrived and turned potatoes to black slime in the ground. Over the following years about **1 million** people died and around **1 million** more emigrated, and Ireland's population fell by roughly 20 to 25 percent. During the famine Ireland continued to export grain, cattle and butter to Britain, while the government in London relied on market forces and limited relief. Ireland's population has still not returned to its pre-famine level of about 8.5 million.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed the danger of depending on one crop, and of a government that would not intervene.
spotlights.memory_hook: One potato, one mould, one million dead, one million gone.

spotlights.name: The Bengal famine of 1943
spotlights.spot_it: Grainy newspaper photographs of starving families on the streets of Calcutta, published by The Statesman in August 1943.
spotlights.story_md: Between about 2 and 3 million people died in Bengal, by most estimates. A cyclone and crop disease had cut the 1942 rice harvest, and Japan's occupation of Burma ended rice imports. But food was still being moved and hoarded. Wartime inflation sent rice prices soaring beyond the reach of labourers and fishermen, and the colonial government gave priority to supplying Calcutta and the war effort, and denied for months that there was a famine at all. When The Statesman, a British-owned paper, printed photographs of the dying in August 1943, it forced the story into public view. Historians still debate how much blame rests with Churchill's war cabinet.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the defining modern example of a famine caused by policy and prices more than by lack of food.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rice existed; people could not afford it, and their rulers looked away.

spotlights.name: Amartya Sen
spotlights.spot_it: An Indian economist with white hair and glasses, often photographed at Harvard or Santiniketan.
spotlights.story_md: Sen was a boy at Santiniketan, Tagore's school, when the famine came; he later recalled starving people passing through. His 1981 book **Poverty and Famines** studied Bengal, Ethiopia, the Sahel and Bangladesh and showed that food supply in Bengal in 1943 was not exceptionally low. What collapsed was the purchasing power of particular groups. He also argued that democracies with a free press avoid famine because governments that face elections and newspapers cannot ignore mass starvation. He received the Nobel memorial prize in economics in 1998. His work changed how governments, including India's, design famine relief and food rations.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He moved the question from 'is there enough food?' to 'who can get it?'.
spotlights.memory_hook: Famines are not about food; they are about who is allowed to eat.

sections.title: Science changes the menu
sections.intro_md:
For most of history food was seasonal and local. Three inventions of the 19th and 20th centuries broke both limits.

First, preservation. Canning, invented for Napoleon's armies, let food keep for years and travel anywhere. Refrigerated ships, from the 1880s, let mutton from New Zealand and beef from Argentina reach London. Food could now be produced on one side of the world and eaten on the other.

Second, fertiliser. Plants need nitrogen, and for all of history farmers got it from manure, legumes or mined guano and saltpetre. In 1909 Fritz Haber found how to make ammonia from the nitrogen in air, and Carl Bosch scaled it up. That one reaction now feeds roughly half the people alive.

Third, breeding. In the 1950s and 1960s scientists bred short, stiff wheat and rice that could take heavy fertiliser without falling over. The Green Revolution that followed doubled and tripled yields across Asia and Latin America, and saved India from the famine many experts predicted for it in the 1960s.

spotlights.name: Nicolas Appert and the first canned food
spotlights.spot_it: A French confectioner's glass bottles sealed with cork and wire, boiled in water to keep the food inside.
spotlights.story_md: In 1795 the French government offered a prize of 12,000 francs for a way to preserve food for armies and navies. Nicolas Appert, a Paris confectioner, spent about 14 years experimenting. His method was to seal food in glass bottles and boil them. It worked, though nobody knew why: Louis Pasteur would only explain the role of microbes some 50 years later. Appert received the prize in 1810 and published his method. The same year, an Englishman patented the idea using tin cans. Oddly, the can opener was only invented decades later; early cans were opened with hammer and chisel.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made food independent of season and place, and fed armies, explorers and cities.
spotlights.memory_hook: Canned food came 50 years before anyone could explain it, and the can opener came even later.

spotlights.name: The Haber-Bosch process
spotlights.spot_it: A tall steel reactor column, and a stern German chemist with pince-nez spectacles.
spotlights.story_md: Air is about 78 percent nitrogen, but plants cannot use it in that form. In 1909 Fritz Haber showed that nitrogen and hydrogen, squeezed together at about 200 atmospheres and heated over a catalyst, form ammonia. Carl Bosch of BASF turned the bench experiment into a factory by 1913. Haber received the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The process now consumes about 1 to 2 percent of the world's energy, and a 2008 study estimated it feeds about 48 percent of humanity; roughly half the nitrogen atoms in your body passed through a Haber-Bosch reactor. Haber also led Germany's poison-gas programme in the First World War.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without it, the world could feed only about half of today's population.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bread from air: half the nitrogen in your body was made in a factory.

spotlights.name: Norman Borlaug
spotlights.when: Wheat breeding in Mexico from 1944; Nobel Peace Prize 1970
spotlights.spot_it: An American agronomist in a cap, squinting in a wheat field, often holding a sheaf of short-stemmed wheat.
spotlights.story_md: Borlaug spent two decades in Mexico breeding wheat that resisted rust disease, then crossing it with a Japanese dwarf variety so the plants would stay short and not collapse under heavy grain. He moved seed between two Mexican sites to grow two generations a year, halving the breeding time. In 1965 and 1966 India and Pakistan imported tens of thousands of tonnes of his seed. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970, the only agricultural scientist so honoured. He is often credited with saving a billion lives, a figure that cannot be tested but captures the scale. Critics point to heavier water, fertiliser and pesticide use, and lost crop diversity.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His wheat changed the arithmetic of hunger in South Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: A short, stiff wheat that would not fall over held up a billion people.

sections.title: India's food revolutions
sections.intro_md:
In the mid-1960s India was importing millions of tonnes of American wheat under the PL-480 food aid programme, and some Western writers predicted mass famine. Two droughts in 1965 and 1966 made things worse. The country's food policy was being written partly in Washington.

India's answer came in two waves. The **Green Revolution**, led by the agricultural scientist M. S. Swaminathan and the agriculture minister C. Subramaniam, brought Borlaug's dwarf wheat to Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. The **White Revolution**, led by Verghese Kurien, organised millions of small dairy farmers into cooperatives. Within a generation India went from begging bowl to grain exporter, and became the world's largest milk producer.

Both revolutions had costs, which are part of the story: falling water tables in Punjab, heavy fertiliser and pesticide use, and a narrowing of what Indians grow and eat. And there is an older Indian food institution, older than both, that feeds tens of thousands every day for free.

visual.title: India's wheat harvest during the Green Revolution (million tonnes, approx.)

spotlights.name: M. S. Swaminathan
spotlights.spot_it: A slight, smiling Indian scientist in a white shirt, often photographed among wheat or rice plants.
spotlights.story_md: Swaminathan, a plant geneticist trained in Cambridge and Wisconsin, invited Borlaug to India in 1963 and ran field trials of Mexican dwarf wheats. Farmers in Punjab took up the seeds fast. India's wheat harvest rose from about 12 million tonnes in 1964 to 1965 to about 17 million in 1967 to 1968, a jump so dramatic that Indira Gandhi released a postage stamp in 1968 called the 'Wheat Revolution'. Swaminathan later warned about the ecological costs of the model he had helped create, and pushed for what he called an 'evergreen revolution'. He was awarded the Bharat Ratna, posthumously, in 2024.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the main reason India stopped depending on food aid.
spotlights.memory_hook: A wheat harvest so big it got its own postage stamp.

spotlights.name: Verghese Kurien and Amul
spotlights.spot_it: A tall Malayali engineer with glasses; and the Amul plant at Anand with its tall steel milk silos.
spotlights.story_md: Kurien, sent by the government to a dairy at Anand in Gujarat in 1949, stayed to build the Kaira District Cooperative, whose brand became Amul. Farmers, many with just one or two buffaloes, pooled milk in village cooperatives and owned the plants that processed it. His team pioneered making milk powder from buffalo milk. In 1970 the National Dairy Development Board launched **Operation Flood**, funded partly by selling donated European milk powder, to copy the Anand model across India. By 1998 India had overtaken the United States as the world's largest milk producer. Kurien, the 'milkman of India', said he did not like drinking milk himself.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made milk a source of steady cash for millions of small rural families, many of them women.
spotlights.memory_hook: The man behind the world's biggest milk industry did not drink milk.

spotlights.name: The langar of the Golden Temple
spotlights.spot_it: Long rows of people of every background seated on the floor in a vast hall, served dal and roti by volunteers.
spotlights.story_md: Guru Nanak and his successors made the communal kitchen central to Sikhism. Everyone, regardless of caste, religion or rank, sits on the same floor and eats the same food, a radical statement in a society divided by who could eat with whom. Tradition holds that the Mughal emperor Akbar sat on the floor and ate in the langar before meeting Guru Amar Das. At the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar the kitchen serves tens of thousands of free meals every day, and many more on festival days, almost entirely through volunteers and donations. Machines can turn out thousands of rotis an hour.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a living example of food used to break social barriers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Emperor or labourer, everyone sits on the same floor for the same dal.

sections.title: One world, one menu
sections.intro_md:
In the 20th century food went global in a new way. It was no longer only crops that travelled, but brands, factories and recipes. A dish invented in one country could be standardised and sold in a hundred.

Three examples show how it worked. Instant noodles were invented in post-war Japan, and are now eaten more than 100 billion times a year, in India as Maggi above all. McDonald's spread from California to almost every country, but in India it had to drop beef and pork completely and invent new menus. And Britain's favourite curry may have been invented in Glasgow.

Globalisation did not simply flatten cuisines. Again and again, local cooks bent global products to local taste.

spotlights.name: Instant noodles
spotlights.spot_it: A block of wavy, deep-fried noodles in a packet or a styrofoam cup, ready in two or three minutes with boiling water.
spotlights.story_md: Momofuku Ando, a Taiwan-born Japanese businessman, saw long queues for ramen in the hungry years after the Second World War. Working in a shed behind his house in Ikeda, near Osaka, he found that flash-frying noodles dried them and left tiny holes that let them rehydrate fast. Chicken Ramen went on sale in 1958; Cup Noodles followed in 1971. Instant noodles are now eaten more than 100 billion times a year worldwide. Nestle launched Maggi noodles in India in 1983 as a 'two-minute' snack; the 2015 lead scare and nationwide ban, lifted after months, were front-page news across the country.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a single invention that changed what billions of people eat on a busy day.
spotlights.memory_hook: A man in a garden shed fed the planet in two minutes.

spotlights.name: McDonald's India
spotlights.when: First Indian outlet October 1996, New Delhi
spotlights.spot_it: The golden arches on an Indian street, over a menu with the McAloo Tikki and a chicken Maharaja Mac.
spotlights.story_md: When McDonald's opened in India in 1996, it did something it had done almost nowhere else: it took beef off the menu entirely, and pork too, out of respect for Hindu and Muslim customers. It created the McAloo Tikki, a spiced potato patty burger, and the Maharaja Mac, first made with lamb and later chicken. Kitchens were split between vegetarian and non-vegetarian lines, with separate equipment, and staff wear different-coloured aprons. India became one of very few markets where the Big Mac does not exist. The case is taught in business schools as an example of 'glocalisation'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that even the most global brand had to bow to local food rules.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's biggest burger chain came to India and dropped its beef.

spotlights.name: Chicken tikka masala
spotlights.spot_it: Chunks of grilled chicken in a smooth, creamy orange-red sauce, served with naan or rice.
spotlights.story_md: The best-known origin story says that in the early 1970s a customer at the Shish Mahal restaurant in Glasgow complained that his chicken tikka was too dry. The chef, Ali Ahmed Aslam, added a sauce improvised from tomato soup, cream and spices. Others claim earlier versions in Delhi or London, and the dish is close to the older murgh makhani. In 2001 the British foreign secretary Robin Cook called it 'a true British national dish', because it took an Indian dish and adapted it to British taste. Aslam died in December 2021. The dish now appears on menus in India too, a recipe that has crossed the world twice.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how empire and migration create new national foods.
spotlights.memory_hook: Britain's national dish may have been rescued by a tin of tomato soup in Glasgow.

sections.title: Myths about food history
sections.intro_md:
Food history is full of stories too good to check. Some are harmless, some distort how we see the past, and a few are repeated in textbooks. A useful habit: when a food story is very neat, ask who first told it, and when.

The four below are among the most repeated. In each case the real history turns out to be more interesting than the myth. The general rule is that food changes are slow, collective and practical: no single king, explorer or chef usually invents a cuisine, and medieval people were not as foolish about food as we like to imagine.

spotlights.name: Myth: spices hid the taste of rotten meat
spotlights.spot_it: Bright heaps of turmeric, chilli, cumin and cardamom in a market, the kind of display that inspires the story.
spotlights.story_md: The story says medieval Europeans loaded food with spices to cover the taste of spoiled meat. Historians such as Paul Freedman of Yale reject it. Spices were extremely expensive, often costing more than the meat itself; anyone who could afford pepper and saffron could afford fresh meat. Medieval towns also had strict rules about selling bad meat, with punishments for butchers. Spices were status symbols, medicines in the humoral theory of health, and associated with the scents of paradise. Fresh meat was in fact easier to get than we assume: animals were killed close to where they were eaten.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It reminds us not to assume people in the past were stupid.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pepper cost more than the steak; nobody wasted it on rotten meat.

spotlights.name: Myth: 'Let them eat cake'
spotlights.when: Phrase in Rousseau's Confessions, written about 1765
spotlights.spot_it: Marie Antoinette in a towering powdered wig and a silk dress, as painted by Elisabeth Vigee Le Brun.
spotlights.story_md: Marie Antoinette almost certainly never said it. The phrase, in French 'qu'ils mangent de la brioche', appears in Rousseau's Confessions, attributed to 'a great princess', in a passage written around 1765, when Marie Antoinette was about nine years old and living in Austria. Similar stories had been told about other royals. The line became attached to her later, as propaganda against an unpopular foreign queen. The bread anger was real, though: as you saw, the women of Paris did march on Versailles over bread prices.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Myths about food often stand in for real political anger.
spotlights.memory_hook: She was a nine-year-old in Vienna when the cake line was written.

spotlights.name: Myth: Marco Polo brought pasta from China
spotlights.when: Popularised by a US trade magazine, 1929
spotlights.spot_it: Dried pasta shapes in jars: spaghetti, penne, fusilli, the backbone of Italian cooking.
spotlights.story_md: The story that Marco Polo returned from China in 1295 with noodles, which became Italian pasta, does not stand up. The Arab geographer al-Idrisi described a dried pasta industry in Sicily in 1154, more than a century before Polo's return, and Italian records mention pasta earlier than his journey too. The myth seems to have been spread by a 1929 article in the Macaroni Journal, a US pasta industry magazine. China does have a far older noodle tradition: a 4,000-year-old bowl of millet noodles was reported from Lajia in 2005. Pasta and noodles were probably invented independently.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a marketing story can become 'common knowledge'.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sicily had a pasta industry before Marco Polo was born.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
Food is still world history in the making. The forces you met today, trade routes, empire, prices, science, are all visible in this year's news.

**Prices.** The FAO Food Price Index stood at **136.0 points in September 2026**, up 1.5 percent in a month, with cereals 17 percent and vegetable oils 18 percent higher than a year earlier, while dairy was 19 percent lower. **Hunger.** The UN's 2026 report estimated that **645 million** people faced hunger in 2025. **Trade politics.** India banned most wheat exports in May 2022 and non-basmati white rice exports in July 2023, when its rice exports were about 40 percent of world trade; the rice curbs were lifted in 2024, a reminder that one country's policy can move world prices. **New foods.** Meat grown from animal cells won new approvals: cultivated quail in Australia and New Zealand in April 2025 and cultivated salmon in the United States in May 2025, while Italy and several US states have banned it.

The old pattern holds. Who eats, and what, is still decided by climate, technology, money and power.

spotlights.name: Svalbard Global Seed Vault
spotlights.spot_it: A narrow concrete wedge sticking out of an Arctic mountainside, its entrance glowing with a light-art installation.
spotlights.story_md: Dug about 120 metres into a sandstone mountain on Spitsbergen, Norway, the vault is a backup for the world's crop gene banks. It can store 4.5 million seed samples at minus 18 degrees Celsius, and the permafrost keeps it cold even if power fails. Over 1.3 million samples are now deposited, including many from India and from ICRISAT in Hyderabad. The first withdrawal came in 2015, when the research centre ICARDA, forced out of Aleppo by the Syrian war, took back seeds to rebuild its collection in Lebanon and Morocco. Fresh deposits arrive several times a year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the world's insurance policy against losing the crops 12,000 years of farming created.
spotlights.memory_hook: Doomsday's pantry is a concrete door in the Arctic.

spotlights.name: The millet comeback
spotlights.spot_it: Small round grains in reddish brown (ragi), pale grey (bajra) and creamy white (jowar), and the bristly heads they grow on.
spotlights.story_md: Millets were among the first grains farmed in China, Africa and India, and fed much of rural India until the Green Revolution pushed rice and wheat. They need far less water and tolerate heat and poor soil, which makes them attractive in a warming climate. At India's proposal, the UN declared 2023 the International Year of Millets, and the government rebranded them **Shree Anna**. India is the world's largest millet producer. Ragi mudde in Karnataka, bajra roti in Rajasthan and jowar bhakri in Maharashtra are being joined by millet pasta and cookies in city supermarkets.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows food history running in reverse: an old grain returning because of a new problem.
spotlights.memory_hook: The grain the Green Revolution sidelined is back as climate insurance.

spotlights.name: Meat grown from cells
spotlights.spot_it: Meat that looks normal on the plate, grown from animal cells in steel bioreactors rather than from a slaughtered animal.
spotlights.story_md: Singapore was the first country to approve cultivated meat for sale, in 2020. The United States approved cultivated chicken in 2023 and cultivated coho salmon from Wildtype in May 2025. Australia and New Zealand approved cultivated quail from Vow in April 2025, and in February 2025 the UK saw cultivated chicken sold in pet food. At the same time Italy passed a national ban in 2023, and US states including Florida and Alabama banned sale in 2024. Prices remain far above ordinary meat and production is tiny. Like the potato and the tomato, it faces a mix of curiosity and suspicion.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a live test of whether a new food can win acceptance, as the potato once did.
spotlights.memory_hook: The newest meat, like the oldest potato, has to win over the suspicious.

sections.title: Recap: the plate as a map
sections.intro_md:
Here is the whole day in one breath. Farming began about 12,000 years ago in several places at once, and three grasses now give us about 60 percent of our calories. Grain made states possible, because it could be counted, taxed and rationed, and some of the first writing was a beer ration. Rome lived on imported grain and oil. Spices, especially Indian pepper and Banda nutmeg, drew ships around Africa and created the first great multinational companies. After 1492 the Columbian Exchange swapped crops between hemispheres, so chillies reached India and potatoes reached Europe. Sugar, first crystallised in India, drove the Atlantic slave trade and then Indian indenture. Tea and opium linked Bengal, China, Britain and America. Salt taxes sparked protests from France to Dandi. Famines, as Amartya Sen showed, are about access more than supply. Canning, refrigeration, Haber-Bosch and Green Revolution seeds made today's world of eight billion possible.

The next time you eat, try to name three continents on your plate.

spotlights.name: A plate of rajma chawal
spotlights.spot_it: Kidney beans simmered in a tomato, onion and chilli gravy, served over white rice.
spotlights.story_md: Take apart the most ordinary North Indian lunch. The kidney beans are a Mesoamerican crop, brought by the Columbian Exchange. The tomato came from the Andes via Mexico and Europe. The chilli arrived in India with the Portuguese. The onion, garlic and cumin came from Central and West Asia long ago. The rice was domesticated in Asia, perhaps first in China, with a separate story in the Ganges valley. The salt may come from Gujarat's Little Rann, and the ghee from a dairy cooperative built on the Anand model. One plate holds five centuries of trade, conquest and science.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns the whole day into something you can see at lunch.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rajma chawal is a Mexican, Andean, Portuguese and Asian collaboration.

cards.front: When and where did Vasco da Gama reach India?

cards.front: What spice was part of Alaric's ransom from Rome in 408 CE?

cards.front: Name this site and its age.

cards.front: What is Mehrgarh?

cards.front: What is Monte Testaccio?

cards.front: What was Muziris?

cards.front: What did the Treaty of Breda (1667) leave the Dutch and the English?

cards.front: What is the Columbian Exchange?
cards.back: The swap of crops, animals and diseases between the Americas and the Old World after 1492 (term by Alfred Crosby, 1972).

cards.front: Why did chilli spread so fast in India after the 1500s?
cards.back: Easy to grow and cheap, unlike pepper; it arrived with the Portuguese.

cards.front: Where do the words 'sugar' and 'candy' come from?

cards.front: About how many Africans were shipped across the Atlantic, and to grow what above all?
cards.back: About 12.5 million (1501 to 1866), mostly for sugar.

cards.front: What happened at Aapravasi Ghat?
cards.back: About half a million indentured Indians landed in Mauritius, 1849 to 1923, for sugar estates.

cards.front: Why did Britain sell Bengal opium to China?
cards.back: To pay for Chinese tea without draining British silver.

cards.front: Who smuggled tea plants from China to the Himalayas?
cards.back: Robert Fortune, 1848 to 1851, for the East India Company.

cards.front: Salt March: dates and distance?
cards.back: 12 March to 6 April 1930, about 385 km, Sabarmati to Dandi.

cards.front: What is Sen's entitlement idea?
cards.back: Famine happens when people lose the means to get food, not only when food runs out.

cards.front: Great Irish Famine toll?
cards.back: About 1 million dead and 1 million emigrated, 1845 to 1852.

cards.front: What does the Haber-Bosch process do, and how many does it feed?
cards.back: Makes ammonia from air; feeds roughly half of humanity.

cards.front: Who led Operation Flood, and what did it achieve?
cards.back: Verghese Kurien; India became the world's largest milk producer by 1998.

cards.front: Where did black pepper grow originally?
cards.back: The Western Ghats and Malabar coast of India.

cards.front: Why could domesticated wheat not spread without farmers?
cards.back: Its ears do not shatter, so seeds stay on the plant until people harvest and sow them.

cards.front: What is this wild grass?
cards.back: Teosinte, the wild ancestor of maize, Mexico.

cards.front: Where do these potatoes come from?
cards.back: The Andes, where the potato was domesticated near Lake Titicaca.

cards.front: What is chuno?
cards.back: Freeze-dried Andean potato, stored for years; fed the Inca state.

cards.front: What does this early tablet record?
cards.back: An allocation of beer, about 3100 to 3000 BCE, southern Iraq.

cards.front: What is this, and how did it survive?
cards.back: A loaf from Pompeii, carbonised by the eruption of 79 CE.

cards.front: Juvenal said the Roman people wanted only bread and ___.
cards.back: Circuses.

cards.front: Which two spices come from this fruit?
cards.back: Nutmeg (seed) and mace (red web), originally only from the Banda Islands.

cards.back: The Dutch East India Company, 1602 to 1799: an early public company with its own army.

cards.front: How much Old World population growth (1700 to 1900) do Nunn and Qian credit to the potato?
cards.back: About a quarter.

cards.front: Why do visitors leave potatoes here?

cards.front: The first Italian name for the tomato was pomi d'___, golden apples.

cards.front: In a 1545 Aztec price list, what did a turkey hen cost?

cards.front: Where is most of the world's cassava grown today?

cards.front: How did coffee reach India, according to legend?
cards.back: Baba Budan smuggled seven beans from Yemen to Chikmagalur around 1670.

cards.front: What is this image, and why was it powerful?
cards.back: The Brookes slave ship plan, 1788: abolitionists used it to show the trade's horror.

cards.front: How many chests of tea were dumped in the Boston Tea Party?
cards.back: 342, from the East India Company, 16 December 1773.

cards.front: Where is this, and who first brewed its tea?

cards.front: What is this carved from?
cards.back: Rock salt: St Kinga's Chapel, Wieliczka Salt Mine, Poland.

cards.front: Bengal famine of 1943: deaths?
cards.back: About 2 to 3 million, by most estimates.

cards.front: What started the Women's March on Versailles (October 1789)?
cards.back: Anger over the price and shortage of bread.

cards.front: What prize did Nicolas Appert win in 1810?
cards.back: 12,000 francs from the French government, for preserving food in sealed bottles.

cards.front: What did the Dunedin do in 1882?
cards.back: Carried about 5,000 frozen sheep carcasses from New Zealand to London in 98 days.

cards.front: Who is this, and what did he breed?
cards.back: Norman Borlaug: short-stemmed, rust-resistant wheat; Nobel Peace Prize 1970.

cards.front: Who led India's Green Revolution in science?
cards.back: M. S. Swaminathan, with minister C. Subramaniam.

cards.front: What is happening here?
cards.back: Langar at the Golden Temple, Amritsar: free meals for all, seated together.

cards.front: Who invented instant noodles, and when?
cards.back: Momofuku Ando, 1958 (Chicken Ramen).

cards.front: Where does the best-known story place the invention of chicken tikka masala?
cards.back: Shish Mahal, Glasgow, early 1970s.

cards.front: Why is 'spices hid rotten meat' a myth?
cards.back: Spices cost more than meat, and towns punished selling bad meat.

cards.front: What is this building?
cards.back: Svalbard Global Seed Vault, Norway, opened 2008.

cards.front: What was 2023 declared, at India's proposal?
cards.back: The UN International Year of Millets.

cards.front: Who is this?
cards.back: Vasco da Gama, who reached Calicut in 1498.

cards.front: Who is this, and what is he known for?
cards.back: Amartya Sen: famine and entitlement theory, Nobel 1998.

cards.front: Who is this chemist?
cards.back: Fritz Haber, who made ammonia from air (1909).

cards.front: Which compound gives black pepper its bite?
cards.back: Piperine.

cards.back: Birds lack the pain receptor that capsaicin triggers, and they spread the seeds intact.
