best_facts.fact: In 1667 the Dutch kept the tiny nutmeg island of Run while the English kept Manhattan, and many Dutch thought they had the better deal.
best_facts.why_surprising: A speck of spice-growing land was valued above the future New York.

best_facts.fact: Chillies reached India only in the 16th century, on Portuguese ships from the Americas. Before that, Indian heat came from pepper and ginger.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most 'Indian' flavour is a 500-year-old immigrant.

best_facts.fact: Roughly half the nitrogen atoms in your body passed through a Haber-Bosch fertiliser factory; the process feeds about 48 percent of humanity.
best_facts.why_surprising: Your body is partly built from air fixed in a factory.

best_facts.fact: Monte Testaccio, a 35-metre hill in Rome, is made of about 53 million broken olive oil jars.
best_facts.why_surprising: An ancient city's rubbish became part of its landscape.

best_facts.fact: When Alaric besieged Rome in 408 CE, his ransom included 3,000 pounds of pepper.
best_facts.why_surprising: A spice from Kerala was demanded beside gold and silver.

best_facts.fact: The English words sugar and candy both come from Sanskrit: sharkara (gravel) and khanda (a lump).
best_facts.why_surprising: Everyday English sweets carry Indian words.

best_facts.fact: Mehrgarh in Balochistan, South Asia's oldest farming village, has the world's earliest known dentistry: molars drilled 9,000 to 7,500 years ago.
best_facts.why_surprising: The first farmers in the region already had dentists.

best_facts.fact: Gobekli Tepe's carved pillars were raised about 11,500 years ago, 6,000 years before Stonehenge and apparently before farming began there.
best_facts.why_surprising: Monuments may have come before agriculture, not after.

best_facts.fact: Peppercorns from India were found in the nostrils of the mummy of Ramesses II, who died in 1213 BCE.
best_facts.why_surprising: Indian spice reached a Pharaoh's burial over 3,000 years ago.

best_facts.fact: The Bengal famine of 1943 killed about 2 to 3 million people even though food supply was not unusually low; prices, war policy and hoarding put rice out of reach.
best_facts.why_surprising: Mass starvation can happen next to available food.

best_facts.fact: Britain paid for Chinese tea with opium grown in Bengal, and went to war in 1839 to keep the trade open.
best_facts.why_surprising: A cup of tea was funded by drug smuggling.

best_facts.fact: A Scottish botanist in disguise, Robert Fortune, smuggled about 20,000 tea plants and seedlings out of China to the Himalayas around 1848 to 1851.
best_facts.why_surprising: Darjeeling tea began with industrial espionage.

best_facts.fact: Nicolas Appert's canning worked for 50 years before Pasteur explained why, and the can opener was invented decades after the can.
best_facts.why_surprising: People used the technology long before they understood it, or could open it easily.

best_facts.fact: In a 1545 Aztec price list, a turkey hen cost 100 cacao beans and a tomato one.
Verghese Kurien, who made India the world's largest milk producer, said he did not like drinking milk.
best_facts.why_surprising: The milkman of India avoided his own product.

best_facts.fact: Sicily had a dried pasta industry by 1154, recorded by al-Idrisi, well before Marco Polo was born; the Polo story spread from a 1929 US trade magazine.
best_facts.why_surprising: A famous food origin story was marketing.

best_facts.fact: Rome gave free grain to about 200,000 citizens every month, and much of it came from Egypt.
best_facts.why_surprising: An empire's stability depended on a welfare programme for bread.

best_facts.fact: When McDonald's entered India in 1996 it dropped beef and pork completely, and invented the McAloo Tikki.
best_facts.why_surprising: The world's biggest burger chain sold no beef in one of its largest markets.

side_dish.title: Why chillies burn and pepper bites
side_dish.body_md:
Today's history was driven by a handful of molecules. It is worth knowing what they do.

Black pepper's bite comes from **piperine**. Chilli heat comes from **capsaicin**. Both work the same trick: they switch on pain and heat sensors in your mouth, especially a receptor called **TRPV1**, which normally fires when something is hot enough to burn you. Capsaicin opens it at body temperature, so your brain hears 'fire' when there is none. That is why water does not help much: capsaicin is oily and does not dissolve in water. Milk, yoghurt and ghee work better because fats and the protein casein carry it away. Raita and lassi exist for a reason.

Why would a plant make a chemical that hurts? The leading explanation is about who eats the fruit. Mammals chew seeds and destroy them. Birds swallow chillies whole and spread the seeds far away, and birds' version of TRPV1 does not respond to capsaicin. The chilli burns the wrong eaters and rewards the right ones.

Humans broke the deal. We learned to enjoy the burn, perhaps because the brain releases endorphins in response, perhaps because heat makes plain staples like rice and maize more interesting. Some researchers have also linked spice use with hotter climates and argued that spices help fight food-borne microbes, though that idea is debated.

The 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went partly to David Julius, whose team had identified TRPV1 in 1997, using capsaicin as the tool. A Mexican plant that conquered Indian kitchens also helped explain how we feel heat.

offline_task.title: Cook (or order) a world-history thali
offline_task.body_md:
Make or order one ordinary meal today and trace every ingredient. Rajma chawal, a vegetable pulao, a pav bhaji or a plate of idli and sambar all work.

1. Write each ingredient on a list: grain, pulse, vegetables, spices, oil or ghee, salt, sugar, drink.
2. Next to each, write where it was first domesticated. Use today's day: chilli, tomato, potato, maize, cashew, peanut and most beans are American; pepper, cardamom, turmeric and rice belong to Asia; wheat, onion and cumin to West Asia; coffee to Ethiopia; tea to China and Assam.
3. Mark anything that arrived after 1498 with a star. Count the stars.
4. For one starred ingredient, tell someone at the table how it got here: which ship, which empire or which famine.

Most people find that at least a third of a 'traditional' Indian plate arrived in the last 500 years. Write your count in your notebook beside today's date.
